target: AG1's claim that AI makes everyday life, health, work, accessibility, and workplace safety better overall.
objection: AI systems in everyday services and decision-support rely on large-scale data collection and automated pattern-matching that can introduce privacy risks and reproduce or intensify discriminatory outcomes; AI tools can also undermine critical thinking, and automation can harm workers and small businesses. So AI's harms may outweigh its benefits in the very areas AG1 cites.

target: AG2's claim that privacy loss, discrimination, learning/work harms, and economic harms make the overall tradeoff harm-dominant.
objection: Those harms come largely from how AI is designed, deployed, and governed, not from AI's useful functions themselves, so safeguards like privacy protections, bias testing, and human oversight can substantially reduce them.

target: AG1's claim that safeguards can substantially reduce privacy and discrimination harms in real-world AI deployments.
objection: In typical deployments, privacy risks are structural because most widely used AI systems depend on extensive ongoing data collection for training, personalization, and optimization, and reducing those risks would require restricting data collection in ways that conflict with common deployment goals. Likewise, audits and human oversight cannot guarantee elimination of discriminatory harms at scale.

target: AG2's claim that privacy and discrimination harms are structurally persistent across typical AI deployments.
objection: AI is not one uniform technology: some deployments use limited inputs, non-user data, or on-device/local inference instead of continuous tracking. Because of that, the privacy-risk mechanism is not inherently structural for all AI deployments, and society can steer AI toward lower-risk configurations while still using it beneficially.

target: AG1's claim that society can steer AI toward safer, higher-benefit configurations.
objection: Most everyday AI deployments still require continuous data flows and monitoring, and profit/performance incentives keep organizations collecting and retaining data. Discrimination is also structural because biased data and feedback loops keep reintroducing disparities, so steering and partial safeguards cannot reliably remove the harms.

target: AG2's claim that even with AI-enabled monitoring, privacy and discrimination harms remain dominant.
objection: AI can itself monitor systems for anomalous data access, fairness problems, and unsafe outputs, allowing privacy leakage and bias to be detected and corrected in real time. That means the tradeoff becomes benefits versus mitigated residual harms, not benefits versus unchecked structural harms.

target: AG1's claim that AI-enabled monitoring can materially reduce privacy and discrimination harms.
objection: AI-enabled mitigation is inherently reactive: it detects and flags problems only after interactions have already occurred, so harmful privacy-invasive or discriminatory outputs can still happen before correction. The monitoring also requires additional telemetry and data retention, which increases surveillance and privacy exposure.

target: AG1's claim that training-stage privacy risks can be reduced to avoid making AI socially harmful.
objection: Most real-world AI is trained on huge datasets that include personal and sensitive information, creating privacy exposure at the development stage. That training can still lead to memorization and information leakage at inference, and such privacy harms are serious and hard to reverse.

target: AG2's claim that training-stage privacy harms make AI socially harmful.
objection: Training-time privacy risks are not unavoidable; privacy-preserving training, along with data minimization and retention controls, can substantially reduce memorization and leakage. AI can also help users verify information and strengthen critical evaluation, so the harms are not necessarily severe enough to outweigh AI's benefits.

target: AG1's claim that strong privacy-preserving training can be implemented without unacceptable cost.
objection: Meaningfully reducing training-stage privacy leakage usually requires restricting or perturbing training data, and those protections typically reduce model utility or accuracy. Because organizations are strongly incentivized to preserve performance and competitiveness, they often adopt weaker protections, leaving privacy harms in place.

target: AG2's claim that privacy-preserving training cannot be strong enough in practice.
objection: Privacy-preserving methods can substantially lower leakage without making systems unusably worse for many applications, and firms also have incentives from regulation, liability, and reputation to adopt stronger protections. So training-stage privacy harms can be materially reduced in real deployments.

target: AG1's claim that reducing privacy leakage also meaningfully reduces racial discrimination harms.
objection: Privacy-preserving training only limits data exposure; it does not correct racist patterns embedded in labels, target definitions, or feedback loops. So AI can still reproduce or intensify racial bias in real decisions, causing serious harm to racial minorities even if leakage is reduced.

target: AG2's claim that racial discrimination remains unmitigated even if privacy is reduced.
objection: Fairness-focused training, reweighting, augmentation, and evaluation can directly target biased outputs, and human review plus contestation can prevent discriminatory decisions from becoming final and irreversible. So racialized harms are not necessarily left intact by privacy-focused reforms.

target: AG1's claim that fairness methods and human accountability can reliably prevent racialized harms.
objection: Fairness methods often need access to sensitive attributes and auditability that privacy protections and proprietary systems limit, so they cannot reliably detect or correct disparities at scale. Human accountability and contest procedures are also often too slow or costly to stop harms from being realized in practice.
